observation: Bulk data replication across multiple cloud regions and providers is essential for data analytics, disaster recovery, and geo-distributed model serving, yet cloud multicast can be expensive due to per-GB network egress fees and slow due to cloud network constraints. Egress prices vary by up to 23× across region pairs, with intra-cloud egress costing $0.01–$0.19 per GB and inter-cloud egress costing $0.08–$0.23 per GB, and cross-region bandwidth varies by up to 202×. Cloud providers impose per-VM egress/ingress limits (for example, AWS throttles egress to 5 Gbps per VM), so a single source VM is often the bottleneck, while users must still meet target replication times. Existing throughput-oriented multicast optimizers do not handle monetary cost, and existing cost-aware multicast work either ignores throughput or assumes a capacity-based pricing model that is inconsistent with today's per-GB egress pricing.

claims: Data replication and multicast have been extensively studied to optimize throughput and scalability in IP networks, peer-to-peer overlays, and inter-DC networks.
Existing throughput-optimizing techniques for multicast poorly handle the monetary cost of transfers between cloud regions and providers.
Some previous work that considers monetary cost for multicast either ignores throughput or assumes a capacity-based pricing model, whereas modern clouds charge per-GB network egress fees.

claims: Other multicast overlay designs have used MILP formulations for optimizing throughput.

These bandwidth-based MILP formulations cannot be extended directly to per-GB costs because the cost is proportional to the product of allocated bandwidth and replication time, which would make the problem non-linear.

claims: A significant body of prior work uses overlay networks to improve the performance and resilience of one-to-one data transfers in the Internet and peer-to-peer networks.
In clouds, previous work has also leveraged cloud elasticity to further improve transfer performance.
These prior systems do not consider the multi-destination cloud multicast problem, and except for Skyplane, none consider the monetary cost of replication in the cloud.

Skyplane's flow-based throughput model results in ambiguous multicast distribution tree solutions because it ignores the identity of data sent along multiple paths, and its optimizer cannot use multiple distribution trees to alleviate source bottlenecks.

claims: Without replication time constraints, a Steiner Tree minimizes egress cost, but the Steiner Tree problem is NP-hard and many approximations exist.

The Steiner Tree algorithm has been applied in the multicast setting to minimize costs in terms of delay and cloud egress costs.
CloudMPCast minimizes egress costs in cloud bulk data multicast by constructing a Steiner Tree overlay network that avoids low-throughput cross-region paths.
CloudMPCast overlooks VM capacity and per-VM egress/ingress limits in its MILP formulation.
CloudMPCast aims to achieve comparable performance to direct transfers while minimizing cost, unlike jointly optimizing throughput and cost.

solution.idea: The paper's central idea is to treat cloud multicast as cost minimization over an overlay network of elastic cloud VMs, splitting data into stripes and routing each stripe along a replication tree that may pass through ephemeral waypoint regions. This targets per-GB egress pricing by avoiding expensive direct source-to-destination edges and source-node bottlenecks: egress bandwidth is offloaded to waypoint VMs and parallel VMs, while the runtime SLO is met by deciding how many stripes use cheaper but slower paths. To keep the optimization tractable and linear, the formulation reasons about data volume (number of stripes) that can traverse each edge within the deadline rather than about bandwidth allocations, converting throughput budgets into data-volume capacities. The main trade-off is additional VM/instance cost and replication latency from extra VMs and waypoints versus egress savings, so the objective minimizes instance cost plus egress cost under a user-selected time budget; varying the time budget produces a Pareto curve of cost versus replication time.
solution.implementation: Cloudcast's implementation begins with profiling: the control plane measures per-VM cross-region bandwidth between region pairs with iperf3, and reads static provider VM egress/ingress limits. It builds a directed graph G=(V,E) whose vertices are cloud regions and edges are cross-region paths. Given TRANSFER-SIZE, TIME, and STRIPES, the planner solves a MILP with decision variables P_{s,(u,v)} indicating whether stripe s traverses edge (u,v), N_v giving the integer number of VM overlay routers in region v, and auxiliary flow variables F_{s,(u,v)}. The objective is minimize TIME * <COST_VM, N> + (TRANSFER-SIZE/STRIPES) * sum_s <COST_path, P_s>, where the first term accounts for instance cost and the second for egress cost. Constraints enforce that each edge's allocated stripe volume does not exceed CAPACITY_path = <N, BANDWIDTH_path> * TIME; that each region's outgoing and incoming stripe volumes do not exceed EGRESS_VM * N_v * TIME and INGRESS_VM * N_u * TIME; that N_v does not exceed LIMIT_VM; and that P defines valid connected acyclic delivery trees by requiring F to satisfy flow-conservation equations that push |DEST| units from the source to a sink connected to the destinations for each stripe while F is positive only on edges where P is 1. Because the full search space is O(2^{|V|^2 * |STRIPES|}) and infeasible for 71 regions and 10 stripes, three approximations are combined: node clustering groups regions by incoming/outgoing pricing and bandwidth features and keeps roughly 20 representative regions; hop constraining limits paths to at most two overlay hops; and a stripe-iterative greedy approximation solves one stripe at a time, decrementing path capacities and per-region limits before solving the next stripe. After planning, the Cloudcast control plane provisions VMs as overlay routers in each required region, configures them with router programs, and registers chunks (at most 64 MB, carrying a stripe ID) with source overlay routers. Each overlay router runs a DAG of modular operators in a shared-memory filesystem; source routers read data from object stores, optionally compress/encrypt, relay chunks over parallel TCP connections to receiving routers, and finally write to destination object stores. Bounded queues provide backpressure, and chunks with different stripe IDs are processed through separate DAGs so different stripes can be routed along different trees.
